definition: Deserving deep respect because of great age, wisdom, or long service.
example: The venerable oak in the town square has shaded family picnics for three centuries.
nuance: Old or ancient only states age, while venerable adds the honor that a long history or lifetime of service has earned.
prompt: A small college celebrates its two-hundredth anniversary.
options: Alumni returned to honor the venerable institution that had educated their grandparents.
Because it was so venerable, the college lay open to attack from every passing critic in town.
The venerable college had opened its doors only last spring, with ten students and one building.
Visitors mocked the venerable college as a shabby embarrassment unworthy of anyone's notice.
reasons: Two centuries of teaching generations of families earns the school real reverence.
This confuses the word with vulnerable; being exposed to harm is not the same as being honored.
A brand-new school has no long history to earn that kind of respect.
The word carries esteem, so pairing it with scorn and ridicule contradicts it.

practice.prompt: A retired violin teacher visits the music school where she once worked.
options: The venerable teacher quietly accepted bribes to raise the grades of her wealthier pupils.
The venerable teacher was a nervous beginner who had started the job just the week before.
Pupils ignored the venerable teacher, since nobody believed her advice was worth hearing.
Students rose to applaud the venerable teacher, who had trained musicians for decades.
reasons: This confuses the word with venal; taking bribes is corrupt and earns no reverence.
A newcomer with one week of experience has no long record to be honored for.
The word means she is held in high regard, so dismissing her opinions contradicts it.
Long years of devoted service explain why the students greet her with such honor.
